masthead_title: Warsh turns hawkish, the front end reprices, and a weekend strike puts oil back in play
regime_line: Fed Chair Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech read hawkish enough Friday to push September rate-hike odds to roughly 60% and send the 2-year Treasury yield up 14 basis points in a single session -- the sharpest, most flagged move on the whole board -- while a fresh U.S. strike on Iranian targets near the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend puts oil back in play for today's open, a move not yet in this system's own data.
provenance_note: Stated reasons and press framing via web search with named-source attribution (the standing source): CNBC, Axios, PBS News, Semafor, Bloomberg, Yahoo Finance/StockStory, Benzinga, Motley Fool, Gurufocus, 24/7 Wall St., Fortune, Morningstar. No paid services used.
claims_section_html:
Claims ledger — one pending, one reversing, one new

Two claims were live going into this morning; neither resolves cleanly today, which is itself worth reporting plainly rather than forcing a call the data can't yet support.

  • CL-0006 — not yet resolvable. Opened Friday: does Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech read hawkish, tested by whether the 2-year Treasury yield (the market's live poll of Fed expectations) rises 4 basis points or more from Friday's pre-speech close of 4.20%, by Monday 08-31's close. The catch: this brief runs before Monday's close, so the formal test isn't gradable yet — that data lands in tomorrow's pull. What's already known: the yield closed Friday (post-speech) at 4.34%, a 14bp move that clears the bar more than three times over on a same-day basis. That's strong preliminary evidence pointing toward "confirmed," but the claim's own wording ties resolution to today's actual close, so it stays open one more day rather than being called early.
  • CL-0005 — still open (due 2026-09-02), and the picture reversed hard in one session. Thursday's brief had semis (SMH, this system's AI-capex proxy) running 2.41 percentage points ahead of the S&P 500 since the 08-25 baseline — evidence for "durable conviction." Friday's Marvell-driven semis selloff (see Movers, below) erased almost all of that: SMH is now down 0.94 percentage points against the S&P cumulative since 08-25 (script-computed from data/macro_series.csv). Still well inside the -2pp floor that would refute the claim, so it isn't refuted — but a 3.3-point swing in a single day is a reminder that "conviction" claims built on a handful of trading days can move fast. Two trading days remain before grading.

A new conditional claim opened this morning: CL-0007 -- the weekend U.S.-Iran flare-up near the Strait of Hormuz marks a durable supply-risk premium, not a one-day headline spike, tested by whether this system's own oil series (Yahoo CL=F) closes at or above $85.00 on 2026-09-03 (three trading days out). Friday's pre-escalation close was $83.40; today's actual level isn't in this system's data yet (see the story, below).
story_html:
The circulating narrative since Friday has two threads. The first: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as chair landed more hawkish than expected — he said this summer's better inflation readings "do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved" and that markets are "showing few signs of policy restraint," language read across the wires (CNBC, Axios, PBS News) as opening the door to a rate hike rather than the cut many had expected from a new chair. Fed funds futures priced the odds of a September hike at roughly 60%, up from about 56% pre-speech. Coverage (Axios, Semafor) also noted the stance puts Warsh's likely path at odds with President Trump's public preference for lower rates — reported here as press framing, not something this brief's data can adjudicate (§4D). The second thread is newer and less settled: reporting over the weekend (Bloomberg) describes a fresh flare-up in the Strait of Hormuz, with the U.S. military striking Iranian rocket launchers Sunday that were reportedly being readied to mine the waterway, and Brent crude quoted above $90 a barrel in that coverage. This system's own oil series doesn't have a Monday print yet — Friday's close was $83.40 — so that number is reported as attributed context, not as this brief's own verified fact.

Does the state file confirm the Fed story? Cleanly, yes. All three flags on today's board (2-year, 10-year, and 30-year Treasury yields) moved the same direction Friday, with the front end moving hardest: the 2-year rose 14 basis points to 4.34% (higher than all but a handful of days in the past six months, z +1.67) while the 10-year rose only 6bp to 4.73% (z +1.69, today's largest single flag) — a curve that flattened by 8bp on the day (2s10s spread narrowed from 47bp to 39bp), the textbook signature of a hawkish repricing concentrated at the short end rather than a broad risk-off move. The dollar (DXY) firmed 0.54 points to 99.70, and gold — which tends to fall when the market prices a tighter Fed and higher real interest rates — dropped 2.85% to $4,478, the sharpest one-day move on the whole board and a clean second confirmation of the same story. Equities took it in stride rather than panicking: the S&P 500 slipped 0.25% to 7,711.76, still just 1.12% off its all-time closing high, and credit didn't confirm any stress — high-yield spreads (the extra yield lenders demand from junk-rated borrowers) actually tightened another 4bp to 2.63% (z -1.12, comfortably calm). The oil story, by contrast, the data can't confirm or refute yet — which is exactly why it's logged as CL-0007 rather than asserted as today's second headline.
dashboard_lag_note: Observation dates in parentheses where they trail the 2026-08-28 market close: the TIPS real yield, breakeven, both credit-spread series, and SOFR publish a day behind (§5), dated to Thursday 08-27; Fed balance sheet and TGA are the weekly Thursday H.4.1 release, dated to Wednesday 08-26. Flagged rows (⚑): far outside the past-6-months normal range — see the Reading key below.
dashboard_interp_html: Friday's move was a genuine, board-wide event rather than the usual single-basis-point drift this brief has been reporting through Unit 1: the 2-year, 10-year, and 30-year Treasury yields all rose together, but unevenly — 2-year +14bp, 10-year +6bp, 30-year +3bp — which is the front-end-led pattern the curriculum has been building toward: a bigger move at the short end than the long end reads as a repricing of what the Fed does next (a path move), not a term-premium touch. That's what pushed all three onto today's flag list at once. It matters in real terms for anyone with an adjustable-rate loan, a money-market fund, or a CD ladder coming due: the market is now pricing meaningfully better odds of a Fed rate increase next month, not the cut many expected a few months ago. The one clean confirmation outside the rates market: gold — which usually loses ground when real (inflation-adjusted) interest rates rise — fell 2.85%, its sharpest move on the board, exactly the direction this story would predict. Credit stayed unbothered: high-yield spreads (2.63%, dated Thursday) and investment-grade spreads (0.79%) both stayed inside normal range and actually tightened slightly, meaning bond investors aren't demanding extra compensation to lend to riskier companies despite the more hawkish rate outlook — a genuine, if quiet, positive. The overnight reverse repo facility (the parking spot money-market funds use for spare cash) dropped from 0.46 to 0.18 (five-day change), still inside its normal range (z -0.50) and best read as month-end plumbing rather than a signal. Fed balance sheet and Treasury cash balance remain "thin history" series (§4) — directional only, no z-score confidence yet.
movers_html:
How this section works: all 503 S&P constituents scanned mechanically; a stock qualifies only by moving >4% (>2.5% for the 50 biggest) — never by seeming interesting. 12 name candidates and 1 sector divergence qualified Friday; cap is 3 names + a sector note. "Stated reason" is what reporting said, not necessarily what's true.

MRVL -10.28% (216.62, from 241.45) -- what happened: Marvell Technology's largest S&P decline Friday despite beating on both revenue and earnings. Stated reason: fiscal Q2 revenue of $2.74B (+37% y/y) beat estimates and the company raised its fiscal 2027 guidance to roughly $12B and fiscal 2028 guidance to about $18B, including detail on a Google custom-silicon partnership worth up to $12.2B — but investors read the raised outlook as thin on detail relative to sky-high expectations built into a richly valued stock (CNBC, Benzinga, 24/7 Wall St., Yahoo Finance). Why it matters: the most direct AI-capex read-through on the board — a beat-and-raise quarter still selling off hard is evidence that the AI-hardware trade is now priced for perfection, not just growth, and it's most of the reason CL-0005 (the semis-conviction claim) swung against the bulls this week. → Route to NR commentary process: a strong-fundamentals-but-sold-off AI-hardware print is plausibly relevant to AI-capex-cycle thesis monitoring; no position-level view expressed here.

PYPL -12.71% (53.66, from 61.47) -- what happened: PayPal's largest S&P decline Friday and the single biggest move on the whole board. Stated reason: Bloomberg reported that a buyout consortium led by Stripe and Advent International walked away from a roughly $53 billion take-private bid (previously offered at $60.50/share) after the two sides couldn't agree on valuation; the stock had run up about 30% since the deal talk surfaced. Why it matters: largely idiosyncratic to PayPal's own strategic situation -- no clear consumer-spending read-through -- but worth one client-relevant aside: a private-equity consortium walking from a deal after valuation talks stall is exactly the kind of financing-sensitive decision that gets harder to close when long-end borrowing costs are rising, the same story leading today's brief. That's an observation, not a tested claim.

WDAY +5.76% (204.72, from 193.57) -- what happened: Workday's largest S&P gain Friday. Stated reason: fiscal Q2 revenue of $2.65B (+12.8% y/y) and adjusted EPS of $2.75 both beat Wall Street estimates, subscription revenue topped the company's own guidance, and management cited AI products driving over $100M in new annual contract value with AI-related ARR up 200% y/y; the board also authorized a $4B buyback (Yahoo Finance/StockStory). Why it matters: a useful counterweight to Marvell above — evidence that AI spending is showing up as real enterprise-software revenue, the demand side of the capex-cycle question, even on the same day the hardware side (Marvell) sold off on guidance-detail concerns.

Sector note: Communication Services (XLC) beat the S&P 500 by 1.65 percentage points Friday (+1.42% vs. -0.23%), the only sector divergence that cleared this system's mechanical 1.5pp threshold. No single, clearly-attributed catalyst surfaced in this morning's search for the sector-wide move (Alphabet and Meta are its two largest constituents) — reported here as a fact worth watching, not a story this brief can explain yet.
chart_of_day_why: The largest |z| flag on the entire board today is the 10-year Treasury yield (z +1.69, narrowly ahead of the 2-year's +1.67 and the 30-year's +1.59) -- all three moved together Friday after Fed Chair Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech, the clearest board-wide confirmation of this morning's story. The 2-year is arguably the more direct read on Fed expectations (and is what CL-0006 is built to grade), but the mechanical rule picks the single largest flag, and today that's the 10-year by a hair.
tier3_html:
Daily read: a genuinely mixed day for the AI-capex trade. Marvell's beat-and-raise-but-sold-off print (see Movers, above) dragged SMH down 3.47% Friday against the S&P's 0.23% decline, a 3.24-point single-day divergence, and flipped CL-0005's cumulative read from a 2.41-point lead (as of Thursday) to a 0.94-point lag since the 08-25 baseline -- still inside the claim's -2pp refutation floor, but a sharp reminder that a handful of hyperscaler and chip-supplier prints can swing this system's whole capex read in a day. Workday's print, on the same day, argued the opposite direction on the software-demand side. Two trading days remain before CL-0005 grades.

Financing watch: Fortune reported August 29 that hyperscaler bond issuance is now large enough to be described as "reverse crowding out" the U.S. Treasury -- Morningstar separately put 2026 bond issuance backing AI investment above $250 billion, with S&P Global counting a roughly 974% year-over-year jump in hyperscaler and Nvidia-linked issuance through midyear, and Goldman Sachs projecting the same five hyperscalers could issue $250B in 2026 alone, rising toward $400B in 2027. That's a real, attributed data point worth flagging alongside today's long-end yield story -- it's a plausible contributing mechanism to rising long-end rates, not a tested one; this brief doesn't have a way to isolate hyperscaler issuance's specific contribution to Friday's Treasury move from the Fed-speech effect, so it's reported as a mechanism to watch, not a cause asserted. Unit 7 of the curriculum (financing cycles and reflexivity, several units ahead of where the reader is now) is where this system will eventually build the tools to test claims like this properly.
calendar_note_html: No scheduled U.S. economic releases land today (§4E: this Monday edition covers since-Friday's-close, and the calendar itself happens to be empty). The week ahead is heavier, and matters directly to today's tightening story: Tuesday brings ISM Manufacturing (high impact) and JOLTS job openings; Wednesday, ADP private payrolls; Thursday, weekly jobless claims and ISM Services; and Friday, the headline event — August nonfarm payrolls, average hourly earnings, and the unemployment rate (all high impact). That print carries extra weight after last Friday's preliminary annual benchmark revision showed March 2026 payrolls were about 79,000 lower than previously reported (the second straight year of a downward revision, though smaller than February's near-900,000 cut) — a reminder that the "how strong is the labor market, really" question is still unsettled heading into a week where Chair Warsh has just raised the stakes on how the Fed will read it.
concept_unit: Unit 2 · Real vs. nominal decomposition · segment 1 of roughly 6
concept_title: Splitting a Treasury yield into two prices: growth-and-inflation, and time
concept_html: Unit 1 treated the 10-year Treasury yield as one number. It's actually two, added together. The real yield (measured by TIPS -- Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, bonds whose payments adjust with inflation) is roughly what investors demand to lend money for ten years after stripping out inflation -- compensation for giving up the use of their money and taking on the risk that growth disappoints. The breakeven is the market's implied average inflation rate over that same period -- literally the inflation rate at which owning a regular Treasury and an inflation-protected one would earn the same return. Add them together and you get (approximately) the plain nominal yield everyone quotes. It's not exact -- there's a small extra sliver for the liquidity difference between the two bond types -- but it's close enough to be useful. Thursday's data (08-27, the most recent date with both figures published) makes the arithmetic almost exact: TIPS real yield 2.34% + breakeven 2.33% = 4.67%, which was that same day's nominal 10-year yield to the basis point. The payoff: when the nominal yield moves, this decomposition tells you whether markets are repricing growth expectations, inflation expectations, or both -- a very different story for a bond portfolio, or a mortgage client, depending on which one moved.
client_translation: "When we say the 10-year Treasury yield, that number is really two things stacked together -- what investors want to be paid for expected inflation, and what they want to be paid on top of that for tying up money for ten years -- and separating them tells us whether a rate move is really an inflation story or a growth story."
client_lens_html:
• "Is the Fed raising rates now instead of cutting?" -- A fair question after Friday. Chair Warsh's Jackson Hole speech read hawkish, and futures markets moved the odds of a September hike to roughly 60% from about 56%. Worth being direct: this is a real, data-confirmed shift (the 2-year Treasury yield, the market's clearest live poll of Fed expectations, jumped 14 basis points Friday), not a headline overreaction -- but it's also not a decision, and this brief logged it as a claim (CL-0006) to grade against tomorrow's actual data rather than calling it today.
  • "Did you see Marvell/PayPal/Workday?" -- Three of the largest S&P moves Friday, in three different directions and for three different reasons: Marvell fell despite beating estimates (guidance detail disappointed elevated expectations); PayPal fell on a collapsed buyout, not earnings; Workday rose on an enterprise-AI-driven beat. Useful illustration that "the market was down 0.25%" can hide very different stories underneath.
  • "What's happening with oil / the Middle East?" -- Reporting over the weekend describes a fresh U.S.-Iran flare-up near the Strait of Hormuz and oil prices moving higher in response. This brief's own data doesn't have a Monday oil print yet (Friday's close was $83.40), so rather than repeating a headline number this brief can't verify, it's logged as a claim (CL-0007) that tomorrow's data will grade.
